analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety enforcement and raises penalties for workplace safety violations.
analysis.headline: The House labor committee approved the mine safety bill 30-17, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have strengthened enforcement of federal mine safety law: mines with repeated safety violations could be shut down until fixed, penalties would rise sharply, and miners idled by a safety shutdown would get full pay for up to 60 days instead of only the rest of one shift. It also raised fines and prison terms under OSHA — the law covering nearly every workplace — for employers who knowingly cause a worker's death or serious injury. The House labor committee approved it 30-17, but the full House never voted before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Miners at chronically unsafe mines, families of accident victims, and the broader workforce covered by OSHA. A mine with a pattern of serious citations could be ordered to pull every worker out until problems were fixed, with eight inspections a year instead of the usual four, doubled fines for repeat failures, and a public database of its record [S3]. Miners idled by a shutdown would be paid in full for up to 60 days [S3]. Miners and other workers would get stronger protection from being fired for refusing dangerous work or reporting hazards, with civil penalties of $10,000 to $100,000 for retaliation [S3]. Accidents killing three or more miners would get an independent investigation panel, modeled on the boards that investigate plane crashes, whose findings and recommendations would be published [S3]. Criminal penalties for knowingly disabling a safety device or exposing miners to a significant risk of death would rise to as much as $2 million and 10 years in prison [S4].

how_it_helps.text: Mines with recurring citations, withdrawal orders, accidents, or injuries would be placed in 'pattern status,' triggering an order to withdraw all workers until the mine is remediated, eight inspections per year, doubled civil penalties for continued failures, and operator-paid fees to cover the extra inspections [S3].

Every accident involving three or more deaths would get an independent investigation panel appointed by HHS, which would identify causes — including operator, contractor, and regulator failures — and publish recommendations to prevent recurrences at other mines [S3].

Miners idled by a safety withdrawal order would receive full pay at their regular rate for the entire shutdown, up to 60 days, instead of current law's coverage of only the balance of the shift plus four hours; the same pay protection would apply when an operator closes a mine in anticipation of an order [S3].

Miners could not be fired or discriminated against for refusing, in good faith, to perform work they reasonably believe is a safety or health hazard, and retaliation against anyone reporting violations would carry civil penalties of $10,000 to $100,000 and up to 10 years in prison [S3].

Title VII would raise civil penalties under OSHA, add criminal penalties for employers whose knowing violations cause a worker's death or serious bodily harm, and give employees victim rights in enforcement proceedings — protections that extend to workplaces across the whole economy [S3].

Underground coal mines would have to brief every miner on hazardous conditions before each shift, raise rock dust levels to 80 percent to prevent explosions, adopt atmospheric monitoring systems, and give miners nine hours of annual refresher training including one hour on their legal rights [S3, S4].

analysis.who_pays: Mine operators bear most of the direct cost: doubled civil penalties while in pattern status, fees for the additional inspections, up to 60 days of full pay for idled miners, personal civil and criminal liability for directors, officers, and agents who knowingly authorize violations, and new equipment and monitoring requirements [S3, S4]. Employers across all industries face higher OSHA civil penalties and, for the first time, criminal exposure for knowing violations causing serious bodily harm as well as death [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The costs fall on operators: doubled penalties for pattern-status mines that miss performance benchmarks, fees to fund eight inspections a year, and up to 60 days of full pay for miners idled by a shutdown — obligations that arrive regardless of whether an individual violation was a paperwork slip or a life-threatening condition [S3, S4].

The bill tilts the process toward the government: the review commission and courts must defer to the Labor Secretary's decisions to approve, modify, or revoke a mine's operating plan unless the operator proves the decision was arbitrary or capricious, and a miner found to have a non-frivolous retaliation complaint would be reinstated immediately, before any final ruling on the merits [S4].

Higher OSHA civil penalties and new criminal exposure for knowing violations that cause serious bodily harm apply to employers in every industry, not just mining, raising the cost of enforcement cases even for employers facing contested or marginal citations [S2].

The three-year job protection at pattern-status underground coal mines bars firing hourly miners without 'reasonable job-related grounds' and lets a court award reinstatement and compensatory damages, which limits operator discretion over routine discipline at the worst-performing mines [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but are aimed mainly at the worst-performing mines: inspection fees, doubled penalties, and shutdown pay obligations attach only to mines in pattern status or subject to withdrawal orders, while the equipment and training requirements apply industry-wide. Set against the recurring deaths from mine explosions and collapses that the bill's enforcement tools were designed to prevent, the bill's design placed its heaviest burdens on operators with documented records of repeated violations. The serious process objections — court deference to the Secretary and immediate reinstatement of retaliation complainants — shift the burden of proof toward operators rather than eliminating it, but they are genuine costs for employers in contested cases.

outcome.mechanism: The House labor committee approved it 30-17 and placed it on the House calendar in July 2010, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 1, 2010, by Rep. George Miller and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S6].
The committee held a hearing on July 13, marked the bill up on July 21, and voted 30-17 to order it reported with amendments [S6].

On July 29, 2010, the committee reported the bill (Report 111-579), it cleared a brief sequential referral to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting House floor action [S6].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a House floor vote, never reached the Senate, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S6, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mine operators and OSHA-covered employers came out ahead: none of the higher penalties, shutdown-pay obligations, inspection fees, or new criminal exposure ever took effect, and enforcement continued under the weaker rules the bill was written to replace.

sides.party_line_note: All 55 cosponsors were Democrats, no Republicans cosponsored, and the committee's 30-17 vote to report the bill showed near-unanimous committee opposition to reporting on the other side.

industries.note: The bill targets the operators with the worst safety records: pattern-status mines would face forced shutdowns, eight inspections a year, doubled fines, and inspection fees, and executives who knowingly authorize violations would become personally liable civilly and criminally. Its costs fall directly on the companies whose mines were the hazard to miners.

Title VII raises civil penalties, adds criminal penalties for knowing violations that cause a death or serious bodily harm, and strengthens anti-retaliation rights for workers in every workplace subject to federal occupational safety law.

industries.industry: Mine safety equipment and monitoring technology vendors
industries.note: The bill would require atmospheric monitoring systems in underground coal mines and direct-reading dust monitors once certified, creating a market for continuous gas monitoring and dust measurement equipment that serves the same goal as the bill's safety mandate.
